title: Human Geography
summary: Explore how people live across the Earth: key geographical concepts and maps, population change and structure, migration, urbanisation and cities, economic geography and development, and resources, environment and fieldwork.
audience: Geography students, teachers, planners and anyone interested in people and places

body.p: Human geography studies how people live across the Earth: where they live and why, how they move, how they use land and resources, and how places are connected. It links closely with economics, sociology, politics and environmental science, and uses maps, data and fieldwork.

list: Place: the meaning and character of a location for the people who live there.
Space: how things are distributed and arranged across areas.
Scale: local, regional, national and global perspectives; a process may look different at each scale.
Interdependence: places are linked through trade, migration, communication and environment.
Human-environment interaction: people adapt to and change their environments.

body.p: On a 1:50 000 map, 1 cm represents 50 000 cm, or 0.5 km. A distance of 4 cm on the map is 2 km on the ground; 2.5 cm is 1.25 km. Geographic information systems (GIS) combine maps with data to analyse patterns, such as clinic locations compared with population density.

body.tip: Look at a map of your area and ask why things are located where they are: markets, schools, roads and settlements.

body.p: Population geography studies the size, distribution, structure and change of populations.

list: Natural increase = birth rate - death rate. With 35 births and 8 deaths per 1000 people a year, natural increase is 27 per 1000, or 2.7% a year.
Doubling time is roughly 70 divided by the growth rate in percent: at 2.7%, about 26 years.
Population density = population / area: 30 million people on 300 000 km² is 100 people per km², though people are rarely spread evenly.
Dependency ratio = (people aged 0 to 14 + people aged 65 and over) / people aged 15 to 64 x 100. If 40% are under 15, 3% are 65 or over and 57% are of working age, the ratio is about 75.4.

body.p: As countries develop, death rates usually fall first (better health and food), then birth rates fall (education, especially of girls, urbanisation and access to family planning). Many African countries have young, fast-growing populations, which can bring a "demographic dividend" of economic growth if young people gain education and jobs.

body.tip: Population pyramids show age and sex structure at a glance; a wide base means a young, growing population.

body.p: Migration is the movement of people from one place to another to live. It can be internal (rural to urban) or international, voluntary or forced.

list: Push factors at the origin: unemployment, conflict, drought, poor services, persecution.
Pull factors at the destination: jobs, safety, education, family, better services.
Intervening obstacles: distance, cost, borders, laws.
Networks: people often follow relatives and friends who moved before them.

body.p: Migration brings labour and skills to destinations and sends remittances (money transfers) home; remittances to many African countries are a major source of foreign income, sometimes exceeding aid. It can also cause "brain drain" of skilled workers and pressure on urban services. Refugees and internally displaced people fleeing conflict or disaster need special protection under international law.

body.tip: Study migration at several scales: a family's decision, a region's labour market and global economic patterns.

body.p: Urbanisation is the growing share of people living in towns and cities. Africa has the fastest urban growth rates in the world, through both migration and natural increase within cities.

list: Central business districts with offices and shops.
Industrial areas, often along transport routes.
Residential areas varying from wealthy suburbs to informal settlements.
Peri-urban areas where city and countryside mix.
Informal settlements lack secure tenure, water, sanitation and safe housing; upgrading programmes improve services in place.
Traffic congestion: investment in public transport such as bus rapid transit (BRT) systems in Lagos, Dar es Salaam and Johannesburg.
Waste and pollution: better collection and recycling, often with informal waste pickers.
Jobs: much urban employment is in the informal sector.

body.p: Good urban planning considers transport, land use, services and climate risks such as flooding together.

body.tip: Map a short walk in your town, noting land uses; you will see urban geography patterns at work.

body.p: Economic activities are often grouped into sectors: primary (extracting resources: farming, mining, fishing), secondary (manufacturing and construction), tertiary (services such as trade, transport, health and education) and quaternary (knowledge-based work such as research and IT). As economies develop, employment typically shifts from primary towards tertiary sectors.

list: Raw materials, markets, labour, transport, energy and government policy influence where industries locate.
Clusters form where related firms gain from being close together, such as technology hubs in Nairobi, Lagos and Cape Town.
Ports and corridors, such as transport corridors linking landlocked countries to the sea, shape regional economies.

body.p: Development is measured with indicators such as GDP per person, the Human Development Index (health, education and income), poverty rates and access to services. Spatial inequality exists between and within countries, for example between capital cities and remote rural areas. Explanations include geography, history (including colonialism), institutions, investment and global trade patterns.

body.tip: Use several indicators together; a single number such as GDP per person hides inequality.

body.p: Human geography examines how societies use land, water, energy and other resources, and the consequences for people and environments.

list: Land use: farming systems, deforestation, land tenure and conflicts over land.
Water: access, irrigation and shared river basins such as the Nile.
Energy: from biomass and fossil fuels to hydro, solar and wind.
Climate change: affects rainfall, food production, health and migration, with the greatest impacts often on those who contributed least to it.
Sustainable development: meeting present needs without compromising future generations.

body.p: Geographers collect primary data through surveys, interviews, traffic counts, land-use mapping and photographs. A traffic count of 12, 8 and 6 vehicles in three 5-minute periods gives 26 vehicles in 15 minutes. Present results with maps, graphs and analysis, and reflect on limitations.

body.tip: Plan fieldwork with a clear question, safe methods and permission from the people involved.
